title: Fix async enrich execution prematurely releases enrich policy lock

timeline.message: Fix async enrich execution prematurely releases enrich policy lock
timeline.author: James Baiera

timeline.body:
When submitting an enrich policy execution with `wait_for_completion=false`, the master node that services the request needs to wait on the remote task to complete so that it may unlock the policy for further runs. It currently does not set a timeout for the Get Task API call, which has a default timeout of 30 seconds. This is almost never enough time to cover an executing enrich policy. At the end of the timeout, the policy is unlocked without any further logic applied. This leaves the new enrich index that is under construction open to be deleted by the background maintenance task.

This PR is a quick fix for the problem. It ups the timeout on the get task API and adds additional logic in the event that the task await call fails.

fixes #94690

timeline.body: Hi @jbaiera, I've created a changelog YAML for you.
I'm not keen on an infinite timeout here. It feels like there should be a better way to ensure that a task on a remote node concludes correctly without setting an infinite timeout.

reply.body: Given discussions offline there's not really a better way to do this at the moment, so I'm leaving it in.

timeline.body: Do we only hit this after TimeValue.MAX_VALUE? Or is this hitting another timeout somewhere?

reply.body:
During normal execution, yeah, this shouldn't really ever receive a timeout because of how long it is configured, but this was the condition that was causing the original bug, so it was the easier place to build a test around.

I think it might be more reasonable to put a lower timeout in (maybe an hour?) just to keep the connection from holding forever, but if the task is stuck on the remote node, then a retry loop likely won't be any more graceful than waiting forever.
I think I'm just going leave the timeout as max value, but keep the timeout handling logic in place for sanity's sake.

timeline.author: James Baiera

timeline.body: This threw me off but I think it's irrelevant -- the case we're actually testing here is when `waitForCompletion` is `false`, right? But since the test's client always returns a response with a task and no status, it doesn't actually matter what is set for `waitForCompletion` here. It might be good just for clarity though to set it to `false` here, and/or update the client to return a status instead of a taskId if it is true.

reply.body: This just puzzled me as well - combination of copy paste gone awry and distraction. It seems that the test works fine because the logic that controls if we return a task id to the client immediately is based on the response from the client when submitting the internal policy action, which we override in the test to respond as if wait for completion was set false. I have updated the test to pass in a false and to verify that it was false.

timeline.body: Can we just assert that `enrichPolicyLocks.lockedPolices().contains(testPolicyName)` here? I assume not, or you wouldn't have gone to the trouble of writing the if block. But I'm not sure how it's possible to get in there, and I haven't been able to after dozens of attempts running the code. Maybe a comment here describing how it's possible to get in the if block?

reply.body: I can try and clarify the comment. The reason this isn't a simple assert call is because if the assertion fails for any reason in the future (hopefully it never does!) there is some cleanup we can do to keep the test failure output from being a mess of multithreaded error logs. Hence the inside of the block.
